claims.text: High-temperature stability of near-equiatomic, multi-element nanoparticles is governed by a synergy between high configurational entropy and severe lattice distortion.
Atomic-size mismatches among constituent elements cause severe lattice distortion.
The initial nanoparticles are homogeneous, near-equiatomic, single-phase solid solutions.
An additional element can be selected that increases lattice distortion without substantially changing configurational entropy.
Inert or reducing atmospheres minimize oxidation during high-temperature annealing.
Configurational entropy thermodynamically stabilizes the single solid-solution phase against intermetallic formation or phase segregation.
Increased lattice strain from atomic-size mismatch lowers atomic diffusivity.
Reduced atomic diffusivity prevents high-temperature reordering and phase segregation.
Nanoparticles with enhanced lattice distortion will retain a homogeneous single-phase structure better than undoped baseline nanoparticles after identical annealing.
Enhanced-distortion nanoparticles will exhibit less phase segregation and a more uniform elemental distribution than the baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies throughout the stated catalytic and thermoelectric temperature ranges when oxidation and other extrinsic reactions are minimized.
The dopant's effects on lattice strain and diffusivity may change outside the stated temperature ranges.
The quantitative effect of dopant-induced lattice distortion on diffusion kinetics and phase stability is composition-dependent and not established.
XRD, TEM, and EDS can be used to compare phase formation, structural integrity, morphology, and elemental homogeneity after annealing.
A lack of statistically significant improvement, or equal or greater segregation in the enhanced-distortion group, would falsify the proposed dominance of entropy–distortion synergy.
